Sorry, I've only tried mssql+pyodbc (which is what we use in production) and tested on sqlite (as a reference).

I'm very glad to see you have restored pymssql to the continuous integration tests using FreeTDS!  When I was looking at which driver to use, it had been dropped, but I also noted some other issues (around unicode) which meant I opted for pyodbc, but I do think it is an important alternative.  I'm also not setup (yet) to test the ODBC Driver 18  for SQL Server (although a move we should probably take soon).  Note also, we don't see the issue with sqlalchemy 1.4.47 (using the same driver and pyodbc) so I'm assuming an sqlalchemy code change somewhere.

I will do what I can on the testing front (but rather tied up now given the time tracking to this stage): I also felt better to raise early.  I'll update if I find some time.
Send use_insertmanyvalues=False to create_engine, that's certainly where the problem is and if pyodbc is not reliable for this we may have to release with the feature turned off for SQL server.
Yep, that fixes the test case sent (sqlalchemy 2.0.8 using mssql+pyodbc).  I will update the production system and report back, but given the nature of the problem I'm suspecting all will be well.
not sure if you noticed that the 2.0 version runs in 2 seconds whereas the 1.4 version goes on and on....  the improvement is very dramatic.   so hope we can keep this

One option we have is to generate the ids code side (which will probably give us some boost in performance).  Would the use_insertmanyvalues=False affect those inserts as well?  I'm guessing this is only an issue when waiting for value of the auto generated ids (from server side).

Thinking aloud, does this break the ODBC standard?  Is there anything you would recommend that I can do to raise with microsoft?

Initial testing on the original production code shows no issues (sqlalchemy 2.0.8 with use_insertmanyvalues=False).  We have a bigger dataset to test aswell, but that will take a day or two, so please consider the issue resolved as far as we are concerned -- but more than happy to do what we can going forward.

SQL Server has an undocumented behavior of running in the rows for an INSERT in an order that is not what was passed in.  our insertmanyvalues scheme assumed (silly us) that the order of the table-valued-expressions would be maintained in the actual INSERT.       When there are somewhere over 100 rows and there are columns that are constrained by foreign key, SQL Server groups rows with common FK values together and reorders how the INSERTs proceed.      

we likely have to add an explicit counter as we insert, which should be doable.  however it means the ORM unit of work is not actually able to insert rows in the order they were given in cases such as these.    I think if we can get the counter to work, we'd then have to document that SQL Server will do this.

here's a demo

```py
from sqlalchemy import Integer, insert, Column, String, create_engine, ForeignKey
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base

Base = declarative_base()


class Datum(Base):

    __tablename__ = "datum"

    datum_id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    data = Column(String(10))


class Result(Base):

    __tablename__ = "result"

    result_id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)

    lft_datum_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey(Datum.datum_id))

    # use this instead to resolve; FK constraint is what affects SQL server
    # lft_datum_id = Column(Integer)


cnxn_url = (
    #"mssql+pymssql://scott:tiger^5HHH@mssql2017:1433/test"
    "mssql+pyodbc://scott:tiger^5HHH@mssql2017:1433/"
    "test?driver=ODBC+Driver+13+for+SQL+Server"
)
engine = create_engine(cnxn_url, echo="debug")


Base.metadata.drop_all(engine)
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)


# size needs to be 13 or greater.  below 13, order is maintained
# I guess just grep the source code for SQL Server for the number 13 :)
size = 13

conn = engine.connect()

result = conn.execute(
    insert(Datum).returning(Datum.datum_id),
    [{"data": f"d{i}"} for i in range(size)],
)

datum_ids = [row[0] for row in result]
assert datum_ids == list(range(1, size + 1))

# the rows are not inserted in the order that the table valued expressions
# are given.  SQL Server organizes the rows so that the "datum_id" values are
# grouped
result = conn.execute(
    insert(Result).returning(Result.result_id, Result.lft_datum_id),
    [{"lft_datum_id": datum_ids[num % size]} for num in range(size * size)],
)

we_expect_returning_is = [
    {"result_id": num + 1, "lft_datum_id": datum_ids[num % size]}
    for num in range(size * size)
]
what_we_got_is = [
    {"result_id": row[0], "lft_datum_id": row[1]} for row in result
]
assert we_expect_returning_is == what_we_got_is

```

sure, this is a gigantic surprise behvaior that they do not document in any way at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/insert-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver16 or https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/queries/table-value-constructor-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver16 , where this syntax is documented.   this is a huge thing they'd have to confirm

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **main** branch:

**turn off use_insertmanyvalues for SQL Server** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/4549

for playing with the INSERT syntax, here's a flat test that uses the SQL string directly

```py
from sqlalchemy import Integer, insert, Column, String, create_engine, ForeignKey
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base

Base = declarative_base()


class Datum(Base):

    __tablename__ = "datum"

    datum_id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    data = Column(String(10))


class Result(Base):

    __tablename__ = "result"

    result_id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)

    thing = Column(Integer, default=5)
    lft_datum_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey(Datum.datum_id))

    # use this instead to resolve; FK constraint is what affects SQL server
    # lft_datum_id = Column(Integer)


cnxn_url = (
    "mssql+pyodbc://scott:tiger^5HHH@mssql2017:1433/"
    "test?driver=ODBC+Driver+13+for+SQL+Server"
)
engine = create_engine(cnxn_url, echo="debug")


Base.metadata.drop_all(engine)
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)


# size needs to be 13 or greater, which means 169 rows or more with the
# scheme used here.
size = 13

conn = engine.connect()

result = conn.execute(
    insert(Datum),
    [{"data": f"d{i}"} for i in range(size)],
)

datum_ids = list(range(1, size + 1))


data = [(num, datum_ids[num % size]) for num in range(size * size)]
flattened_data = []
for t, l in data:
    flattened_data.extend([t, l])

result = conn.exec_driver_sql(
    f"""
    INSERT INTO result (thing, lft_datum_id)
    OUTPUT inserted.result_id, inserted.lft_datum_id, inserted.thing
    VALUES {', '.join('(?, ?)' for i in range(size*size))}""",
    tuple(flattened_data)
)


we_expect_returning_is = [
    {"result_id": num + 1, "lft_datum_id": datum_ids[num % size], "thing": num}
    for num in range(size * size)
]
what_we_got_is = [
    {"result_id": row[0], "lft_datum_id": row[1], "thing": row[2]} for row in sorted(result, key=lambda r: r[2])
]
assert we_expect_returning_is == what_we_got_is

```

yeah the JSON thing of course is another option.  but this is not the code we have, we'd have to write something totally new.   can pyodbc support this with returning maybe ?
also json encoding is a whole crazy ballgame that im not too comforable with as a top-level replacement for INSERT

So would the select be an option?
The Microsoft doc suggests it if you want to insert more than 1000 rows at once, since insert values has am hard limit at 1000
it doesnt work.  it puts the rows in the table in random order but returns the RETURNING in PK order, so we can't line up our records w/ the returning

Ok, so definitely not in values order :(

Does not seem to be a way. I've tried putting a variable in the output list and it works, but I don't know how to populate it wirh a value from the values
